841.title: The wheel the earth held
841.hook: Karna's wheel sinks and his weapon slips away, as two old deeds come due
841.carry: karma: even an accident bears fruit
841.tomorrow: Karna calls out to wait. will anyone listen?
841.howItsDone: Many Hindu pujas close with a short prayer asking pardon for any fault done knowingly or unknowingly. The scene of Karna on foot, straining to lift his sunken wheel, is retold in recitations, plays and serials of the Mahabharata, along with the curses behind it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna nearly drew his sword on his own brother, and Krishna showed him a way through. Your line was dharma upholds life; truth serves it.

Karna and Arjuna, at last, face to face. Karna fits a terrible arrow to his bow, an arrow with a serpent in it, the epic says, a snake with an old grudge against Arjuna. Shalya, at the reins, gives him advice: aim for the chest. Karna refuses. He doesn't aim twice, he says, and he looses at Arjuna's head. And Krishna, driving the other chariot, presses down with his feet, and the chariot sinks into the earth, just enough. The serpent arrow takes Arjuna's crown and leaves Arjuna alive. Hold on to that sinking chariot.
screen: `THE SERPENT ARROW.` → `AIM FOR THE CHEST.` → `KRISHNA PRESSES DOWN.`

segments.voice: The duel goes on, and then the earth takes hold of Karna's chariot wheel. It sinks, and it stays sunk. In the same moment Karna reaches in memory for his greatest weapon, and the words are gone. The epic explains both with old deeds. Years before, Karna had killed a Brahmin's cow by accident, and the Brahmin cursed him: when you most need it, the earth will swallow your wheel. And as a young man Karna had trained under the great teacher Parashurama, hiding who he was. When the teacher found out, he cursed him to forget that weapon in the hour he needed it. Two old debts, come due on one afternoon. The earth that saved Arjuna now holds Karna fast. Hindus call it karma: every act is a seed, and it ripens in its own time. Karna never meant to kill that cow, and the fruit came anyway. Intention matters, and Hindu teachers weigh it, but an act still leaves its mark. That's one reason many pujas end with a short prayer asking pardon for anything done wrong, knowingly or unknowingly. Not guilt for its own sake: a habit of owning even the harm you didn't mean. Karna jumps down and grips the wheel with both hands: the commander of an army, on foot, straining at a wheel.
screen: `THE EARTH HOLDS THE WHEEL` · `TWO OLD CURSES` · `KARMA: EVERY ACT IS A SEED` · then, large: `PARDON FOR WHAT WE DIDN'T MEAN`

segments.voice: Sit tall, both feet on the floor. Let one small harm come to mind that you never meant: a careless word, a forgotten promise, a moment you weren't paying attention. If you pray, ask pardon for it in your own words, and for the ones you don't know about, the way many Hindus close their worship. If you don't pray, simply own it to yourself, and choose one small way to make it right.
Karna. The warrior whose wheel sinks and whose weapon slips from memory, when two old deeds come due on one afternoon.
Your line: karma, even an accident bears fruit. That's why the prayer asks pardon for what we didn't know we did. Until tomorrow.

842.title: Now you remember dharma?
842.hook: Karna appeals to the rules of war, and Krishna answers with questions
842.carry: dharma is lived, not just claimed
842.tomorrow: after Karna, is it too late for peace?
842.howItsDone: Karna's death is retold in readings, regional theater, poems and serials, and Karna is discussed as a figure hard to judge: generous, loyal, wronged at birth, and complicit in wrong.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karna's wheel sank into the earth and his weapon slipped from memory. Your line was karma: even an accident bears fruit.

Wait. That's what Karna calls out, standing on the ground with his hands on the wheel. Wait, Arjuna. A warrior in a chariot shouldn't strike a man who is on foot, whose wheel is stuck, who isn't ready. Those are the rules of fair fighting, he says, in effect. Remember dharma. Give me a moment to free the wheel. By the rules the armies agreed to, it sounds like a fair request, made by a man in real trouble. And it isn't Arjuna who answers. It's Krishna, from the driver's seat.

Krishna's answer is a string of questions. Now you remember dharma, Karna? Where was it when Draupadi was dragged into the assembly hall and you mocked her? At the rigged game of dice? When young Abhimanyu was surrounded by many warriors at once and cut down? And Krishna adds, in effect: people in trouble blame fate, never their own deeds. In Ganguli's English, Karna hangs his head in shame, and says nothing. He climbs back into the stuck chariot and fights on. Then Arjuna, urged on by Krishna, takes up a single great arrow, and Karna falls. The epic gives one more picture: a light rises from his body into the sun, his father. Here's what Hindus take from it. Dharma isn't a rulebook you open only when you're losing. It's a way of living, and the life you've lived is what answers when you call on it. Karna knew the rules of fair fighting perfectly; he just hadn't kept them for others. And notice the epic doesn't make him a cartoon villain. Hindus still call him daanveer Karna, Karna the great giver, the man who gave away his own armor. Both are true, and the story holds both. One more thing. The Pandavas, cheering, still don't know who just died. Kunti knows. Her sons will learn after the war that they have killed their eldest brother.
screen: `NOW YOU REMEMBER DHARMA?` · `KARNA HANGS HIS HEAD` · `DHARMA IS LIVED, NOT CLAIMED` · then, large: `A BROTHER THEY DIDN'T KNOW`

segments.voice: Krishna made Karna look back at his own deeds. Sit quietly and let today replay: one moment you kept faith with someone, and one moment you didn't. Don't build a defense; let the quiet after it stay quiet. If you pray, offer both moments to God in your own words. If you don't pray, just name them honestly to yourself.
Karna. The wheel stuck, the questions he couldn't answer, the light rising into the sun, and brothers who didn't yet know him.
Your line: dharma is lived, not just claimed. Karna asked for a fairness he hadn't given. Day eight hundred forty-two, done.

843.title: It isn't too late
843.hook: after Karna, an old teacher pleads for peace, and Duryodhana says no
843.carry: it is never too late to turn toward dharma
843.tomorrow: who should face the new commander? not who you'd think.
843.howItsDone: The Shalya Parva, the epic's book named for Shalya, is read and recited with the rest of the Mahabharata; Kripa's plea for peace and Duryodhana's refusal are retold as a turning point before the war's last day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karna died beside his stuck wheel, with Krishna's questions still in the air. Your line was dharma is lived, not just claimed.

Karna is gone. Bhishma lies on his bed of arrows. Drona is dead. The commanders Duryodhana trusted have fallen one after another, and in the Kaurava camp the king sits among the survivors, grieving. Then an old man speaks up. It's Kripa, the teacher who trained these princes when they were boys, Kaurava and Pandava alike. He doesn't flatter. He tells the king the truth as he sees it.
screen: `KARNA IS GONE.` → `THE COMMANDERS HAVE FALLEN.` → `KRIPA SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Kripa's counsel, in Ganguli's English, is plain: make peace with the Pandavas. Yudhishthira is gentle, he says in effect; he will still agree. There's still time. And Duryodhana says no. His reasons are worth hearing. I've wronged them too deeply, he says; they'd never trust a peace from me now. And my friends died for me. How could I live in comfort after sending them to die? So Drona's son Ashvatthama names a new commander: Shalya, king of Madra, the man who drove Karna's chariot, and this book of the epic takes his name. Now the teaching. Kripa's words are the Hindu answer, and Duryodhana's are the trap. It is never too late to turn toward dharma. In the Bhagavad Gita, spoken by Krishna on this same battlefield, he says that even someone of very bad conduct who turns to him with a whole heart is to be counted good, because he has resolved rightly. Later retellings remember a forest robber who turned and became the sage Valmiki, the poet of the Ramayana. Duryodhana's real enemy isn't the Pandava army. It's the voice that says, I've gone too far to be trusted, so I may as well keep going. The door Kripa held open was real. Duryodhana just couldn't believe it was open for him.
screen: `KRIPA SAYS MAKE PEACE` · `DURYODHANA SAYS NO` · `THE GITA: TURN, AND YOU ARE COUNTED GOOD` · then, large: `THE DOOR IS STILL OPEN`

segments.voice: Sit tall. Bring to mind a road you've stayed on because turning back would mean admitting something. Kripa's point is that the turn is still open. If you pray, offer that road to God in your own words, or with the name you use for God. If you don't pray, picture one small step back the way you came, and notice that it is still there to take.

844.title: The dice-master's last day
844.hook: the patient brother faces Shalya, and the dice-master meets Sahadeva
844.carry: dharma is restored, in its own time
844.tomorrow: the last king is alone. where does he go?
844.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's battle with Shalya and Sahadeva's killing of Shakuni are told in the Shalya Parva and in retellings and serials of the Mahabharata, as the moment the war's last vows begin to be kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Duryodhana turned down Kripa's plea for peace, and Shalya took command. Your line was it is never too late to turn toward dharma.

Who should face Shalya? On the Pandava side, the question goes to Krishna, and his answer is not the obvious one. Not Arjuna. Not Bhima. Yudhishthira: the eldest brother, the one who lost everything at dice, the one Karna sent back to camp humiliated just the day before. Shalya is strong, Krishna says, in effect, and you are the one to meet him. Put away your gentleness for today. And Yudhishthira, the man the epic keeps showing us as patient, picks up his weapons.
screen: `WHO SHOULD FACE SHALYA?` → `NOT ARJUNA. NOT BHIMA.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA.`

segments.voice: The fight is long and fierce, and in Ganguli's English the patient king is almost unrecognizable: steady, fearless, pressing forward. At last Yudhishthira hurls a dart, a spear made for throwing, with all his strength. It strikes Shalya, and the king of Madra falls. The twins have lost their uncle. As Shalya's army breaks, another fight finishes something older. Shakuni, Duryodhana's uncle, the man who threw the dice in the rigged game, is still on the field. In the dice hall, years before, the youngest brother Sahadeva had sworn that Shakuni would die by his hand. Now Sahadeva finds him. The dice-master has no dice here, and the vow from that hall is kept. Twelve years in the forest, a year in hiding, eighteen days of war, and the wrong done at a gaming table is finally answered. Many Hindus hear a teaching in a day like this. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says: whenever dharma declines and adharma rises, I come, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back in its place. Notice what that promises, and what it doesn't. Not that wrong never wins: Shakuni won, for years. Only that it doesn't get the last word. Hindus hold on to that when cheating seems to pay. Dharma is restored, in its own time, not always in ours. And Duryodhana, looking around, finds himself almost alone.
screen: `SHALYA FALLS` · `SAHADEVA FINDS SHAKUNI` · `AGE AFTER AGE, DHARMA RESTORED` · then, large: `WRONG DOESN'T GET THE LAST WORD`

segments.voice: Sit tall and let your face soften. Bring to mind one wrong that seems to be winning, in your life or in the news, and don't rehearse the anger. If you pray, hand it to God, the way Hindus lean on Krishna's promise, and ask for patience and for the part that's yours to do. If you don't pray, name one small thing you can do for what's right, and leave the rest for now.
Shalya. The commander who falls to the patient eldest brother, while Sahadeva settles an old vow with the dice-master Shakuni.
Your line: dharma is restored, in its own time. The quiet brother remembered. See you tomorrow.

845.title: The king under the lake
845.hook: the last Kaurava king walks into a lake, and some hunters overhear
845.carry: sakshi: every deed has a witness
845.tomorrow: the hidden king makes an offer. should they take it?
845.howItsDone: Duryodhana's hiding in the lake, told in the Shalya Parva, is retold in readings, regional theater and serials of the Mahabharata, and the lake scene leads into the war's final duel.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shalya fell to Yudhishthira's dart, and Sahadeva kept his vow against Shakuni. Your line was dharma is restored, in its own time.

One man walks away from the battlefield on foot, carrying a mace. His horse is dead. His army is gone. His brothers, his friends, his commanders have fallen. He is the king the whole war was fought for, and he is alone. On the way he meets Sanjaya, his father's companion, and gives him a message for the blind old king at home: tell my father I've gone into the lake. Then Duryodhana walks down to the water's edge, and keeps walking.
screen: `ALONE, ON FOOT.` → `TELL MY FATHER.` → `INTO THE LAKE.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's English, Duryodhana enters the lake and, by a power of illusion he knows, binds the waters around him so he can rest beneath them, hidden. The lake lies smooth and still, and the last Kaurava king lies under it. Three survivors of his army find the lake: Kripa, Ashvatthama and Kritavarma. They call down: come out, fight with us. From under the water he answers: not tonight. I'm wounded and tired. Then some hunters pass, men who bring meat to Bhima's kitchen. They hear a king talking from under a lake, and they know the Pandavas are searching for him, so they go and tell Bhima. The Pandavas come with Krishna, and Yudhishthira calls to the still water: why are you hiding? Duryodhana answers from below: I'm not afraid. I'm only resting. Here's the teaching. Much earlier in this same epic, Shakuntala tells a king who pretends not to know her: you think you alone know what you did. But the sun and moon, wind and fire, earth, sky and water, your own heart, day and night, and dharma itself witness what a person does. Hindus call that witness sakshi. It's why a Hindu wedding vow is made with Agni, the fire, as witness. Duryodhana hid in the one place he thought no one could see, and the water was a witness too. The lake kept his body. It couldn't keep his secret.
screen: `HE BINDS THE WATERS` · `THE HUNTERS OVERHEAR` · `WHY ARE YOU HIDING?` · then, large: `SAKSHI: EVERY DEED IS WITNESSED`

segments.voice: Let your body grow still, the way a lake does when the wind drops. Bring to mind something you do when you think no one's watching, kind or not so kind. Hindus say God dwells in every heart as the inner witness. If you pray, offer it there, in your own words. If you don't pray, picture it in plain daylight, and ask whether you'd still choose it.
Shalya. The book of the war's last day: the commander fallen, and Duryodhana lying hidden under a lake until hunters give him away.
Your line: sakshi, every deed has a witness. Even the water saw. Day eight hundred forty-five, done.

846.title: One more throw
846.hook: Duryodhana offers the earth; Yudhishthira refuses, then stakes everything again
846.carry: samskara: old habits cut deep grooves
846.tomorrow: two cousins, two maces. who taught them both?
846.howItsDone: The exchange at the lake, from the Shalya Parva, is retold in readings and serials of the Mahabharata, and Duryodhana's earlier refusal of even a needle's point of land is recalled there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Shalya book, Duryodhana lay hidden in the lake until some hunters gave him away. Your line was sakshi: every deed has a witness.

An offer rises from under the water. Take the whole earth, Duryodhana says, in effect. My friends are dead, my brothers are dead. I have no wish to rule an empty kingdom. I'll go to the forest, dressed in deerskins, and live there. It sounds like surrender, the end of the war handed over without another blow. And Yudhishthira, standing on the bank, refuses.
screen: `TAKE THE WHOLE EARTH.` → `I'LL GO TO THE FOREST.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA REFUSES.`

segments.voice: It isn't yours to give, Yudhishthira answers, in Ganguli's telling. Before the war you wouldn't give us as much land as the point of a needle would cover. Now that you've lost it, you offer it all as a gift? A warrior doesn't take a kingdom as charity. Come out and fight. Then he goes further. Choose any one of us, he says, with any weapon you like. Beat that one, and the kingdom is yours. Krishna is alarmed. You've staked everything again on a single throw, he says in effect; none of you but Bhima can face Duryodhana with the mace, and even Bhima has less skill. Some readers hear the old dice game here: the king who lost everything once by gambling has just gambled again. Hindu thought has a word for that pull: samskara. Every act leaves an impression in the mind, and impressions repeated become grooves, so the next act slides the same way. Yudhishthira is the dharma king, wise and truthful, and the groove of the dice is still in him. It's one reason Hindu practice leans on the daily: a morning prayer, a name repeated on the mala, a lamp lit at dusk. No single day is magic. Repeated good acts cut new grooves. Duryodhana rises out of the lake, dripping, mace on his shoulder, and he chooses the mace. And Bhima steps forward to meet him.
screen: `IT ISN'T YOURS TO GIVE` · `CHOOSE ANY ONE OF US` · `SAMSKARA: THE OLD GROOVE` · then, large: `DAILY PRACTICE CUTS NEW GROOVES`

segments.voice: Japa is an old Hindu practice: one name or mantra, repeated, often on a mala of a hundred and eight beads. Sit easy, hands open. If you pray, repeat a name of God you love, quietly, for the rest of the sit: Ram, Krishna, Om, whichever is yours. If you don't pray, repeat one short word you want more of, like peace. Each time the mind slides off, bring it back. That's a new groove being cut.

847.title: On the field of dharma
847.hook: a teacher walks onto the field just as his two best students raise their maces at each other
847.carry: dharmakshetra: life is the field of dharma
847.tomorrow: the teacher saw the blow. what will he do?
847.howItsDone: The mace fight between Bhima and Duryodhana is a favorite scene in retellings, dance-dramas and recitations of the Mahabharata. Kurukshetra, which takes in Samantapanchaka, is a pilgrimage place today, and pilgrims bathe in its sacred tanks such as Brahma Sarovar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Shalya book, Yudhishthira refused the earth offered from the lake and staked everything on one fight. Your line was samskara: old habits cut deep grooves.

Two men face each other on open ground, each holding a heavy iron mace. One is Bhima, of the Pandava brothers. The other is Duryodhana, the Kaurava king, wet from the lake he hid in. Just then a third man arrives, fresh from a long pilgrimage along the holy river Sarasvati. It's Balarama, Krishna's elder brother. He taught both of these men how to fight with the mace. He has stayed out of the whole war. Now he's back in time to watch his two students try to kill each other.
screen: `TWO MEN, TWO MACES.` → `A TEACHER ARRIVES.` → `BOTH ARE HIS STUDENTS.`

segments.voice: Balarama greets everyone and asks for the fight to move. In Ganguli's telling, they walk to Samantapanchaka, ground held holy, so that a warrior who dies there dies in a sacred place. It lies in Kurukshetra. Then the cousins close in, circling like bulls. At the edge, Arjuna asks Krishna which is better. Bhima is stronger, Krishna says; Duryodhana has more practice and more skill. Fought by the rules, Bhima may not win. Then Krishna reminds Arjuna of the dice hall, where Duryodhana bared his thigh to Draupadi, and Bhima vowed to break it. Arjuna, where Bhima can see him, strikes his own thigh. Bhima sees. When Duryodhana next leaps, Bhima swings low, a blow the rules of mace fighting forbid, and breaks both his thighs. The king falls. Now the teaching. The Bhagavad Gita opens with a blind king asking about this very place: on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, what did my sons and Pandu's sons do? Dharmakshetra, the field of dharma. Kurukshetra is a pilgrimage place to this day, and pilgrims bathe in its sacred tanks. And many teachers read the field inward too: later in the Gita, Krishna calls the body itself a field. Your own life is where dharma gets kept or broken, choice by choice, even when the right blow and the forbidden one are inches apart. And the teacher of both fighters has seen all of it.
screen: `MOVE TO HOLY GROUND` · `ARJUNA STRIKES HIS OWN THIGH` · `THE BLOW BELOW THE WAIST` · then, large: `DHARMAKSHETRA: THE FIELD OF DHARMA`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your thighs and feel the legs that carry you all day. Bring to mind the place where your hardest choices happen this week: a classroom, a kitchen table, a phone screen. If you pray, ask God to stand with you on that field, in your own words. If you don't pray, simply call it what the Gita calls Kurukshetra, a field of dharma, and notice how you'd walk in.
